content: Bromophenol blue, also known as Tetrabromophenolsulfonephthalein, is a chemical compound that functions as an acid-base indicator. Its effective pH range as an indicator spans from 3.0 to 4.6. Within this range, bromophenol blue undergoes a reversible color change, appearing yellow at a pH of 3.0 and transitioning to purple at a pH of 4.6. In addition to its role as a pH indicator, bromophenol blue is widely utilized as a color marker in electrophoretic techniques, such as agarose gel electrophoresis and polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis. Due to its slight negative charge at moderate pH levels, bromophenol blue migrates in the same direction as DNA or proteins during electrophoresis. The migration rate of bromophenol blue is influenced by factors such as gel density and the composition of the buffer. For instance, in a standard 1% agarose gel prepared with TAE (Tris-acetate-EDTA) or TBE (Tris-borate-EDTA) buffer, bromophenol blue migrates at a rate comparable to that of a DNA fragment approximately 500 base pairs in size. Other dyes, such as xylene cyanol and Orange G, may also serve as alternative markers for this purpose. The molecular weight of bromophenol blue is approximately 670 Daltons (or grams per mole). It is also employed as a dye in various applications. At neutral pH, bromophenol blue absorbs red light most strongly, resulting in a blue appearance due to the transmission of blue light. Conversely, at low pH levels, the dye predominantly absorbs ultraviolet and blue light, giving it a yellow appearance in solution. When dissolved in water without pH adjustment, bromophenol blue exhibits a characteristic green-red color at a pH of 3.6, which lies in the middle of its transition range. This phenomenon, where the dye displays two distinct colors depending on the viewing conditions, is referred to as dichromatic coloration. Bromophenol blue is also commonly used in introductory laboratory courses to stain proteins on wet-mount slides, facilitating their visualization under a microscope.
